newsitem.title: USA: Group wants spinal cords banned from meat processing.
newsitem.headline: Group wants spinal cords banned from meat processing.

text.p: A consumer group Wednesday prodded the U.S. Agriculture Department to ban beef companies from processing spinal cords because of the risk "mad cow disease" could enter the nation's food supply.

"If mad cow disease is present in U.S. herds there is nothing to prevent it from getting into the food supply because there is no restriction on the use of spinal cord," said Caroline Smith DeWaal, director of food safety at the Centre for Science in the Public Interest.

The Washington-based group wrote the department asking for a rule that beef processors must remove the thick cord of nerve tissue from the spinal column before feeding cattle carcasses into high-tech machines that strip meat from bone.
CSPI said aside from the brain, the spinal cord is the most infectious part of an animal with BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy), or the so-called mad cow disease.

Recently, scientists have linked BSE to a new variant form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, a fatal degenerative neurological disorder affecting humans. The newly identified JCD, which leaves spongelike holes in the brain, has killed 10 people in Britain.

There have been no reported cases of BSE in the United States. Last week, the Food and Drug Administration moved to protect U.S. livestock from the disease by banning the practice of feeding reprocessed animal tissue to other animals.
"Government scientists can't guarantee that 'mad cow' disease is not in this country," said DeWaal. "American consumers should receive at least as much protection from BSE as American cows receive."

The group charged the department has not sufficiently tested for the disease. "While USDA inspects over 33 million head of cattle per year, it has only tested 5,100 cattle brains for BSE since 1986," it said in a letter dated Jan. 7.
The Agriculture Department is in the midst of reviewing its regulations on meat and bone separation machinery in response to other concerns raised by consumer groups and industry.
"We will consider their comments as part of the whole rulemaking process," said Jacque Knight, spokeswoman for the department's Food Safety and Inspection Service.

Current rules do not allow spinal cords to be processed if they are loose but allow it if they are attached to the spinal column. Knight said a department survey showed the spinal cord was usually removed.
In 1995, Britain imposed new controls forbidding any use of the spinal column in "mechanically recovered meat."
Advanced meat recovery machines produce 300 to 400 million pounds of ground meat products each year, which are mixed in with retail ground beef, the consumer group said.
